scale.note: 10 is always the most favourable outcome (Delay 10 = lowest delay, Complexity 10 = simplest, Cost 10 = cheapest).
scale.basis: Baseline scores are the author's analytical assessment, derived from qualitative characteristics in the references. They are not measured or published numerical values.

criteria.name: Architecture / Organization
criteria.best: Clear structure, scalability, ease of expansion

rubric.5: Workable but expansion disrupts service or adds hops
rubric.10: Clear, modular structure that grows without redesign

rubric.1: Long or unpredictable waits that grow with load or size
rubric.5: Acceptable at light load; degrades with size or contention
rubric.10: Minimal hops and bounded, predictable latency

criteria.name: Complexity
criteria.best: Simplest to design, install and manage

rubric.1: Many links/ports per node; hard to install and troubleshoot

criteria.name: Security
criteria.best: Least exposure of traffic to other nodes

rubric.1: Shared medium: every node can observe all traffic
rubric.5: Traffic transits other stations or shared segments
rubric.10: Dedicated links; traffic never transits third parties

criteria.name: Congestion control
criteria.best: Least contention, best behaviour under load

rubric.1: Contention and collisions rise sharply with load
rubric.5: Orderly access but shared capacity or a bottleneck
rubric.10: No shared links or contention-free access

criteria.name: Routing methodology
criteria.best: Most efficient and flexible path selection

rubric.10: Direct path plus alternatives on failure

criteria.name: Reliability
criteria.best: Highest fault tolerance, no single point of failure

rubric.1: One failure stops the whole network
rubric.5: Failures isolated in places, but a single point of failure remains
rubric.10: No single point of failure; traffic reroutes

criteria.name: Cost
criteria.best: Cheapest in cabling, devices and maintenance

rubric.1: Highest cabling, port and maintenance cost
rubric.5: Moderate cabling plus some active devices
rubric.10: Least cabling and no central device

topologies.name: Bus
topologies.how: All stations attach by taps to one shared cable terminated at both ends. Only one station can transmit at a time; classic Ethernet used CSMA/CD to share the medium.
topologies.today: Historic coaxial Ethernet (10BASE5, 10BASE2). Not a modern LAN procurement option; the shared-medium idea survives in some industrial field buses.
topologies.limits: Every frame reaches every station, a cable fault stops the whole segment, and collisions grow with the number of stations.
topologies.description: All stations tap into one shared backbone cable terminated at both ends; access by CSMA/CD.

justification.text: Single shared backbone; passive taps; terminators at both ends
Fine at light load; degrades as collisions grow with more nodes
Simplest topology to install; minimal hardware required
Broadcast medium: every station can see every frame
Contention-based CSMA/CD; collisions rise sharply under load
No routing: frames are broadcast and filtered by address
A backbone cut or terminator fault takes the whole network down
Least cable of all topologies and no central device

topologies.name: Star
topologies.how: Every station has its own link to a central device. With a switch, frames are forwarded only to the destination port; with a legacy hub they are repeated to all ports.
topologies.today: The standard layout of wired Ethernet access networks in offices, homes and campuses.
topologies.limits: The central device is a single point of failure unless it is duplicated. Scores assume a switch, not a hub.
topologies.description: Each station has a dedicated link to a central switch or hub; the dominant LAN design today.

justification.text: Dedicated point-to-point link from each node to a central switch
At most two hops; a switch forwards frames in parallel
Easy to install, extend and troubleshoot node by node
Central point for access control, port security and monitoring
Switch buffers traffic and isolates collision domains
Central switch forwards by MAC table over a single path
Link faults stay isolated, but the hub is a single point of failure
More cable than bus plus the cost of the central device

topologies.name: Ring
topologies.how: Each station connects to two neighbours, forming a closed loop. Frames are repeated from station to station in one direction (dual rings can use both).
topologies.today: Rare in office LANs. Protected rings remain in metro/carrier fibre and some industrial networks.
topologies.limits: Delay grows with ring size, and a single break stops a single ring unless a protection ring or bypass exists.
topologies.description: Each station connects to exactly two neighbours, forming a closed loop; data travels one way.

justification.text: Closed loop of point-to-point links; each node repeats the signal
Delay grows with the number of nodes on the ring
Moderate; adding or removing a node interrupts service
Frames pass through every intermediate station
Orderly sequential transmission, but no traffic prioritisation
One fixed path around the ring; no alternative route
A single node or link failure breaks the ring (unless dual ring)
Only n links and no central device needed

topologies.name: Token-ring
topologies.how: Not a separate physical shape: IEEE 802.5 is a medium-access method. A token circulates on a logical ring, usually wired physically as a star through MSAUs; only the token holder transmits.
topologies.today: Withdrawn IEEE standard, replaced by switched Ethernet. Included for comparison; its idea of deterministic access survives in some real-time networks.
topologies.limits: Specialised, hard-to-source hardware; token management adds complexity. Compared here as a design option, not as an equal modern purchase.
topologies.description: IEEE 802.5: a logical ring, physically star-wired through MSAUs; a circulating token grants access.

justification.text: Logical ring, physically star-wired through MSAUs
Deterministic: maximum waiting time is bounded and known
Token management, active monitor, priorities and beaconing
Frames pass via stations; MSAU allows central control
Collision-free access; very good performance under high load
Sequential forwarding; source routing between bridged rings
MSAU bypasses failed stations; beaconing detects faults
Specialised NICs and MSAUs; legacy, hard-to-source hardware

topologies.name: Tree
topologies.how: Star segments are connected upward to higher-level switches and a root, forming a hierarchy.
topologies.today: The basis of hierarchical campus design (access, distribution, core layers).
topologies.limits: Traffic between branches crosses the upper levels, and the root is a single point of failure unless duplicated.
topologies.description: A hierarchy of star segments joined to a root/backbone; combines bus and star characteristics.

justification.text: Hierarchical star segments; easy to expand branch by branch
Several hops across levels add latency at the root
Manageable per segment, but more devices to configure
Segmentation allows per-branch policies; backbone is exposed
Traffic converges on root and backbone links (bottleneck)
Hierarchical single path up and down the tree
Branch faults stay local; root or backbone failure splits network
More cabling and switches than a single star

topologies.name: Mesh (partial)
topologies.how: Selected nodes have several links to other nodes, so traffic has alternative paths. Path choice is made by routing or switching protocols, not by the cabling alone.
topologies.today: Network cores, WAN backbones, data-center fabrics and wireless mesh networks.
topologies.limits: Its reliability advantage exists only if the redundant links and devices are actually installed and configured.
topologies.description: Critical nodes are interconnected by multiple links; other nodes connect as needed (WAN / backbone).

justification.text: Critical nodes multiply connected; edge nodes linked as needed
Short paths; traffic can take the least-delay route
Needs routing protocols and many links to maintain
Point-to-point links; traffic can avoid untrusted paths
Load is spread over alternate paths
Dynamic, adaptive routing over multiple paths
Redundant paths; traffic reroutes around failures
Extra links and ports raise installation cost

topologies.name: Fully connected
topologies.how: A special case of mesh: every node has a dedicated link to every other node, which needs n(n-1)/2 links and n-1 ports per node.
topologies.today: Practical only for a small number of critical nodes, such as a few core routers or sites; not for end devices.
topologies.limits: Links grow quadratically: 10 nodes need 45 links, 50 nodes need 1,225.
topologies.description: Every node has a dedicated link to every other node: n(n-1)/2 links and n-1 ports per node.

justification.text: n(n-1)/2 dedicated links; scales poorly as n grows
Single hop between any pair; full-duplex links
n-1 ports per node; very hard to install and maintain
Private dedicated links; no transit through other nodes
No shared links, so no contention
Direct path always available, plus alternates on failure
Maximum redundancy; no single point of failure
Highest cabling, port and maintenance cost

limitations: Scores are ordinal judgements on a 1-10 scale; the weighted sum treats them as if differences were equal-sized.
The weighted sum is compensatory: a strong score on one criterion can hide a weak one. Weak points are therefore listed separately.
Complexity and Cost are related, so weighting both highly partly counts the same concern twice.
Security and congestion depend heavily on switching, protocols and configuration (VLANs, QoS, access control), not on topology alone.
Baseline scores do not depend on network size; size effects are handled by explicit scenario rules, not by changing scores.
Results are educational guidance, not an engineering-validated design. Real designs need site surveys, traffic measurements and vendor specifications.
